highlights: The 89th Imperial Diet passed the Trade Union Law, the Agricultural Lands Adjustment Law and an Election Law establishing women's suffrage before it was dissolved.

SCAP issued the Shinto Directive on 15 December, separating State Shinto from government administration, public finance and school curricula; on 21 December it banned militaristic textbooks in morals, geography and history.

Seven directives ordered the arrest of 205 war criminal suspects, bringing Sugamo Prison internments to 445; former Prime Minister Prince Fumimaro Konoye committed suicide on 16 December rather than be arrested.
At Japan's first war crimes trial, at Yokohama, a military commission convicted Tatsuo Tsuchiya of prisoner abuse and sentenced him to life imprisonment.

Eighteen holding companies, including Mitsui, Mitsubishi, Yasuda and Sumitomo, and 325 subsidiaries were designated restricted concerns for dissolution; the Big Four Zaibatsu reported 3.15 billion yen in assets.

Coal production rose 53 percent to 840,000 metric tons while steel stayed at five percent of capacity; Bank of Japan note circulation reached 51.09 billion yen and urban food reserves fell to two-to-eight days.

Announcement of the Moscow Conference's four-power trusteeship plan set off nationwide Korean strikes and mass demonstrations coordinated by Kim Koo's Anti-Trusteeship Committee; free rice marketing was suspended from 1 January 1946.
Lieutenant General John R. Hodge denounced the Korean People's Republic, declaring Military Government the sole lawful governing authority in South Korea.

sections.summary: Japanese politics, public safety and war crimes: the 89th Diet's laws, new parties, Tokyo crime statistics, arrest of 205 war criminal suspects, and the Tsuchiya trial at Yokohama.
sections.title: Part II: Political - Japan

sections.summary: The 89th Diet passed women's suffrage, land reform and trade union laws before dissolution; many parties formed, including the Japan Cooperative and New Japan Women's parties; the Cabinet abolished the Board of Information.
sections.title: Government and Civil Administration

sections.summary: Tokyo crime statistics showed no postwar crime wave; the Economic Police Section was eliminated in police demilitarization; political prisoners regained voting rights; hidden military aircraft engines were seized in Shizuoka.
sections.title: Public Safety and Intelligence

sections.summary: Seven directives ordered arrest of 205 war criminal suspects, bringing Sugamo Prison internments to 445; Tatsuo Tsuchiya received a life sentence at Yokohama; trials of camp commanders Yuri and Furushima began.
sections.title: Legal and War Crimes

sections.summary: Japanese economy: rice collection, coal output of 840,000 tons, steel at five percent of capacity, Labor Union Law, 3.19 million unemployed, 51.09 billion yen note circulation, and eighteen restricted holding companies.
sections.title: Part III: Economic - Japan

sections.summary: Government rice collection lagged at 30 percent of quota, prompting higher purchase prices and subsidies; soil surveys assessed reclamation; naval fuel oil releases boosted fish landings and curbed black-market sales.
sections.title: Agriculture and Fisheries

sections.summary: Operations at Japan's largest modern sawmill and the Amagi Imperial Forest were surveyed; coal production rebounded 53 percent to 840,000 tons; declassified wartime data showed overexpansion in subsidized mining.
sections.title: Forestry and Mining

sections.summary: Steel ran at five percent of capacity; 228 vessels were repaired in shipyards; the textile industry reorganized into a democratic association; the Diet repealed sixteen major wartime industrial control laws.
sections.title: Industry

sections.summary: Coastal tankers carried vital petroleum products; seventeen radio navigation beacons were restored; electric heater use overloaded urban distribution systems; coal shortages limited Tokyo gas service to three hours daily.
sections.title: Transportation and Public Utilities

sections.summary: An Imperial Ordinance created the Board of Trade to manage foreign commerce; imports were limited to salt and kerosene, coal and silkworm eggs were exported, and an inventory of 50,000 silk bales was ordered.
sections.title: Imports and Exports

sections.summary: The Labor Union Law spurred rapid unionization in mining and transport; Yomiuri and Keisei Railway disputes ended with wage increases; occupational registration recorded 3.19 million unemployed.
sections.title: Labor

sections.summary: Trunk cable reconstruction advanced; Sender Composition Message service to the United States handled record holiday traffic; 1946 radio set production was projected at 3.1 million; captured military equipment was stripped for civilian parts.
sections.title: Communications

sections.summary: Urban food reserves fell to two-to-eight days; rice purchase prices and producer subsidies rose; fish ceiling prices were reestablished; petroleum prices surged 280 to 400 percent after subsidy abolition.
sections.title: Rationing and Price Control

sections.summary: Bank of Japan note circulation reached 51.09 billion yen on government advances and commercial borrowing; monthly bank condition reporting began; repatriates could bring in yen savings books and bonds.
sections.title: Money and Banking

sections.summary: Diet supplementary budgets funded food and salt production; military pensions were suspended; the Big Four Zaibatsu reported 3.15 billion yen in assets; SCAP restricted eighteen holding companies financially.
sections.title: Public Finance

sections.summary: Japanese public health, welfare, education, religion and media: DDT against typhus, the 71,996,477 census count, the Shinto Directive, textbook bans, and the 'Now It Can Be Told' broadcasts.
sections.title: Part IV: Social - Japan

sections.summary: DDT dusting checked typhus among Hokkaido coal miners; military hospitals went civilian, doubling bed capacity; the November census counted 71,996,477 residents; a 30,000-person nutrition survey was run in Tokyo.
sections.title: Public Health and Welfare

sections.summary: SCAP issued the Shinto Directive abolishing state sponsorship and banned militaristic textbooks in morals, geography and history; an American educational mission was requested; 'Now It Can Be Told' war history was broadcast.
sections.title: Education, Religion and Media of Expression

sections.summary: South Korea under USAMGIK: anti-trusteeship protests led by Kim Koo, Hodge's repudiation of the Korean People's Republic, rice price ceilings restored, bank mergers, and education and health appointments.
sections.title: Part V: Korea

sections.summary: The Moscow Conference trusteeship announcement ignited Korean strikes and mass demonstrations led by Kim Koo; General Hodge repudiated the Korean People's Republic; a National Bar Association was established.
sections.title: Political Activities in Korea

sections.summary: Despite a 15.97-million-koku rice harvest, market withholding forced suspension of free trading and restored price ceilings; Japanese-owned farmland went to the New Korea Company; Japanese branch banks merged into Korean ones.
sections.title: Economic Activities in Korea

sections.summary: A Korean was appointed Director of Education; Korean Pacific Press began independent operations with Associated Press; Seoul University graduated its first public health class; diphtheria antitoxin was flown in from Japan.

summary: Monthly Summation No. 3 covers non-military activities of GHQ/SCAP in Japan and USAMGIK in southern Korea during December 1945. In Japan, decisive structural reforms reshaped political and social life. The extraordinary Diet session enacted landmark democratic legislation, including the Trade Union Law, the Agricultural Lands Adjustment Law, and an Election Law granting women suffrage. Concurrently, SCAP directives disestablished State Shinto, banned militaristic textbooks, ordered dissolution of eighteen Zaibatsu holding companies, and established the International Prosecution Section. War crimes proceedings intensified with the apprehension of 205 high-ranking suspects—precipitating Prince Fumimaro Konoye's suicide—and the first Yokohama military trial convicting Tatsuo Tsuchiya. Acute coal shortages, currency expansion, and low urban food reserves hindered industrial recovery. In Korea, the Moscow Conference agreement proposing a four-power five-year trusteeship triggered nationwide strikes and mass protests led by Kim Koo, while General Hodge repudiated the authority of the Korean People's Republic. For historians, this report provides crucial statistical baselines from the November 1945 census, primary documentation of demilitarization policies, and essential evidence of early Cold War tensions across Northeast Asia.
